sections.excerpt: Most people think marketing means advertising and promotion. That belief is the reason most marketing money is wasted. If you internalize the correct definition in the next 25 minutes, you will already be ahead of a meaningful share of people who do this professionally.

The definition worth memorizing Marketing is the work of understanding a group of people well enough to build, price, place, and describe something they will choose over the alternatives — profitably and repeatedly. Four things to notice: Understanding comes first. Research is not a nice-to-have that precedes the real work; it is the work. It includes the product itself. What you build and what you charge are marketing decisions, not just engineering and finance ones. "Over the alternatives." Marketing is always comparative. The alternative is often "do nothing," which is the toughest competit

A marketer's actual week looks roughly like: 20% talking to customers or reading what they wrote (support tickets, reviews, sales calls) 20% making things (copy, ads, pages, emails) 20% looking at numbers and deciding what to change 20% coordinating with sales, product, and finance 20% arguing about priorities Not one minute of it is "coming up with creative ideas" in the way films depict. Ideas are the cheap part.

Three shifts that make the fundamentals more valuable, not less: AI collapsed the cost of production. Anyone can produce a thousand competent blog posts and a hundred ad variants. That means execution volume is no longer a moat. Judgment, positioning, and knowing what is worth saying are the moat. Distribution surfaces are consolidating into answer engines. Roughly 60% of Google searches now end without a click to any website, and when an AI Overview appears, the click-through rate of the top organic result drops by more than half. Whole categories of "just rank and get traffic" strategies qui

Confusing marketing with promotion. Leads to fixing an ad when the problem is the price. Copying tactics from companies in a different situation. What works for a brand with existing awareness will not work for you. Always ask: what was true for them that isn't true for me? Optimizing what is easy to measure. Search ads are measurable and often not incremental (see M15) — people would have found you anyway. Brand-building is barely measurable and often decisive. Treating "the market" as one thing. There is no general audience. There are segments (M02). Believing the funnel is orderly. Real buy

List the real alternatives your buyer considers — include "do nothing" and "hire someone / do it manually." Classify your current marketing efforts (or a competitor's, if you have none) into demand capture vs demand creation . What is the split? For each of the 4 Ps, write one sentence about your business. Which of the four is weakest? Be honest — that is where the leverage is. Write down: what would have to be true for this business to double? Name it as

Marketing is the whole system of understanding, building, pricing, distributing, and describing an offer — not the promotion at the end. When something is not working, check the offer before you check the ad.

Positioning, price, channel and copy are guesses until you know who you are for and what they are trying to get done. This is the cheapest skill to acquire and the one most professionals do worst, because it requires talking to strangers instead of opening a dashboard.

Segmentation, and why demographics are usually the worst basis Segmentation is splitting a market into groups that behave differently and should therefore be marketed to differently. The test of a real segment is not "are these people similar?" but "would I say something different to this group?" If no, it is a label, not a segment. Basis Example Verdict Demographic Women 25–34 Same age and income, entirely different reasons to buy. Firmographic (B2B) 50–200 employees, SaaS Correlates with budget, but is not a reason to buy. Psychographic "Health-conscious" Feels insightful, rarely actionable.

A first pass takes about a week of spare hours: find what your 20 best customers share; read 30 competitor reviews and tag recurring phrases; run 5 interviews; write one page — ICP, three jobs, top trigger, top anxiety, ten quotes. Re-run twice a year, or whenever a campaign fails and nobody can say why.

AI makes synthesis cheap and fabrication easy. Clustering 20 transcripts takes minutes now. But "synthetic personas" and AI-generated survey respondents reproduce plausible averages and cannot surface the odd trigger that explains your best customers. Use AI on real data, never instead of it. Platform targeting is dying; audience understanding is not. You no longer hand-pick an interest list — you supply creative and conversion signals. What you say, and who you exclude, are the remaining levers. Privacy changes shrank behavioural data , putting more weight on qualitative evidence you gather y

Hypothetical questions , then treating politeness as demand. The leading cause of launching something nobody buys. Interviewing only current customers. They already chose you; the growth is in those who did not. Segmenting by who people are instead of what happened to them. Averaging. Two segments averaged together produce a product for neither. Confusing user with buyer — common in B2B and anything bought for children or teams.

For your chosen business : Draft the ICP (15 min): trigger, situation, size/budget, current alternative, success conditions, three disqualifiers. Write three jobs in the When… I want to… so I can… format. At least one emotional or social. Get real data (25 min) — either 5 interviews using only past-behaviour questions (write the five first, none hypothetical), or 30 reviews weighted toward 3-star, tagged into trigger / job / objection / delight / deal-breaker. Tally the four forces (5 min): two of each. Circle the biggest blocker — that is your next messaging or offer change. Capture 10 verbat

From memory: Why demographics are a weak segmentation basis, and two better bases What distinguishes an ICP from a persona The JTBD sentence format The four forces, and which two beginners neglect The Mom Test rule in one sentence Four cheap sources of qualitative data
Ask what they did, not what they would do. Define your customer by the situation that made them look, and your competitors by the job, not the category.

Positioning is the decision that makes every later decision easier or impossible. Weak positioning shows up as ads that need three sentences to explain what you are, a sales team inventing its own pitch, and a price you cannot defend. You cannot fix it downstream with better copy.

Positioning is context, not a slogan Positioning is the context you place your product in so its value is obvious to the right person. A hammer is unremarkable in a hardware store and remarkable on a desert island. April Dunford's five components The most usable framework in the discipline. Work it in this order — the order is the method: Competitive alternatives. What would customers do if you did not exist? Include spreadsheets, an intern, an agency, and doing nothing — taken from M02 interviews, not a competitor grid. Unique attributes. What do you have that the alternatives do not? Facts o

Positioning is a two-week job, not a two-hour one: interviews (M02), a session running Dunford's five steps, a draft, then testing it on five people who do not work for you — ideally recent buyers and recent losses. The test is comprehension, not applause: ask them to explain back what you do and who it is for. Then roll it into website, deck, ads and onboarding in the same month, or you will run three positions at once.

Discovery increasingly runs through AI answer engines that summarise a category and name a handful of options. Those summaries are assembled from how you and others describe you: your site, review sites, forums, comparison articles, press. Ambiguous positioning is now a retrieval failure, not only a comprehension failure. If your site never plainly states "X is a [category] for [segment]," a model has nothing unambiguous to lift. Repetition across sources beats clever phrasing on your homepage. The brand that gets named is the one described the same way in many places, so third-party corrobora

Positioning against a competitor instead of the real alternative , which is usually the status quo. Choosing the category you want rather than the one buyers search in. Changing the message because you are bored of it. Internal fatigue arrives long before customer awareness. Claiming three things at once. Nothing lands. Feature lists with no outcome, or outcome fluff with no proof. Positioning by committee — a statement true of everyone and exciting to nobody.

For your chosen business , using the M02 quotes: Run Dunford's five steps in order (20 min): alternatives (include "do nothing") → unique attributes (facts only) → value → who cares most → category. Write the honest version, not the flattering one. Fill the positioning statement template (5 min). One line. Rewrite until it fits. Build the message hierarchy (15 min): one core message, three pillars, concrete proof under each. If a pillar has no proof, find proof or cut the pillar. Delete test (5 min): take your homepage (or a competitor's) and strike every line a competitor could also claim. Wh

From memory: Dunford's five components, in order The positioning statement template Differentiation vs. distinctiveness, and what mental availability means The three layers of a message hierarchy Feature vs. benefit vs. outcome, with your own example Why "we're the best" fails the test
Positioning is a decision about context and exclusion, not a slogan. Decide who you are not for, state it the same way everywhere, and repeat it long past the point where you are sick of it.

Price is the only lever that drops straight to profit — no production cost, no media cost. Most businesses set it by copying a competitor or adding a markup to cost, the two worst methods available. Meanwhile the offer wrapped around the product, and the places it can be bought, move sales more than any campaign.

A product is not an offer The product is what you make. The offer is everything weighed at the moment of decision: the product, price and payment terms , risk reversal (guarantee, free returns, pilot, easy cancellation), the bundle , onboarding and support , real urgency, and proof . Two businesses can sell an identical product at very different conversion rates because one has an offer and the other has a price list. If you cannot change the product you can nearly always change the offer — faster and cheaper than a new campaign. Most offer components are anxiety-reducers (M02), not new benefi

Price gets revisited far too rarely, usually only in a panic. Healthier: review annually and after any material change in cost, competitor set or value delivered. Test increases on new customers first, grandfather existing ones for a period, and announce with a reason and notice. Price rises lose fewer customers than founders fear, and the ones lost are the least profitable.

Comparison is instant and conversational. AI assistants line up prices and alternatives side by side, raising elasticity in commodity categories and rewarding clear published pricing. Hiding price behind "contact us" increasingly means being left out of the comparison. Rising ad costs make margin decisive. Only businesses whose contribution margin can fund a CAC (M05) survive paid acquisition. A price increase is often the fastest way to make a channel affordable. Platform dependence is a live risk. Fee changes and algorithm shifts have killed otherwise healthy businesses. An owned email list

Pricing from cost. Your costs are your business, not the buyer's concern. Competing on price with no cost advantage. A slow retreat, not a strategy. Discounting instead of improving the offer. Guarantees and bundles cost less and do more. Never raising prices while costs rise, then needing a painful 30% correction. One price for everyone when two segments value you very differently. Treating distribution as logistics. It is a marketing decision with the largest multiplier.

For your chosen business : Write the current offer in full (5 min) — product, price, terms, guarantee, bundle, onboarding, proof. Note what is missing. Rewrite it (10 min), strengthening at least two components — ideally a risk reversal aimed at the biggest anxiety from M02. Set a price with written rationale (5 min): buyer's next-best alternative and its cost, value delivered, your cost floor, the position the price signals. One paragraph. Run the discount math (2 min) on your real margin: what volume does a 20% discount require? List every place you can be bought (3 min), plus one you are no

From memory: Six components of an offer beyond the product The three pricing methods and why two are bad What a 20% discount does at 40% gross margin Two signs a market is inelastic When freemium makes sense One reason distribution beats promotion
Fix the offer before you fix the ad, and price against the buyer's alternative rather than your own costs. Then make sure it is genuinely easy to buy.

This is the most important module in Part 1. Everything else is judgement you build over years. This is arithmetic you can learn in ninety minutes, and it decides whether a business survives. Marketers who cannot do this arithmetic get fired, because they cannot answer the only question a CFO ever asks: what did we get for the money, and can we afford more of it?

AIDA and the modern lifecycle AIDA — Attention, Interest, Desire, Action — dates from the 1890s and still describes the sequence of persuasion. The modern version adds what happens after the sale: Awareness → Consideration → Conversion → Retention → Advocacy. Retention and advocacy are where profit lives. Acquisition usually loses money on the first purchase; the business is made on the second and the tenth. The funnel is an accounting fiction Real journeys are not funnels. People enter in the middle, leave, return months later, ask a friend, read reviews, forget, see an ad, then search your b

Build one spreadsheet: traffic, step conversion rates, AOV or ARPU, margin, CAC by channel, retention curve, payback. Update it monthly. Most "should we do X?" questions are answered by changing one cell. When a channel underperforms, diagnose in order — traffic volume, step conversion, order value, margin — and check the model before the creative.

Attribution is much weaker than it was. Privacy changes, cookie loss and platform black boxes make channel-level CAC an estimate. That raises the value of blended CAC, media-mix modelling and holdout tests (M15) over dashboard attribution (M13). Platform-reported conversions are inflated. Ad platforms count every conversion they had a plausible claim to, so summing platform reports usually exceeds actual sales. Reconcile against your own order data. Paid acquisition costs keep rising faster than most price increases, widening the gap between businesses with retention loops (M17) and those rent

Using revenue as LTV. The most common error, and it inflates everything downstream. Chasing traffic when the constraint is conversion — or optimising conversion on 200 visitors. Ignoring payback because LTV:CAC looks good. Excluding salaries and tools from CAC , then wondering why the P&L disagrees with the dashboard. Averaging across segments. One profitable cohort can hide three unprofitable ones.

For your chosen business — real numbers if you have them, honest estimates labelled as estimates if not: Build the funnel (15 min): traffic → key intermediate step → conversion → repeat purchase, with a rate on every arrow. Contribution margin per customer (5 min): price minus every variable cost. LTV24 (5 min): contribution per month or per order × a conservative 24-month retention assumption. Max affordable CPA (10 min), backwards as in example 2: target CAC → max cost per lead → max cost per click. Compare with real CPCs in your category. Is any paid channel affordable today? Work backwards from what a customer is worth in contribution margin to what you can afford to pay for a click. If the answer is below the market price of traffic, no amount of creative or optimisation fixes it — change the price, the conversion rate, or the channel.

Almost everything called a marketing strategy is a list of tactics with a budget attached. It cannot be argued with, because it makes no claim about why those tactics will work. This module gives you the structure that makes a plan defensible — and the artifact you show an employer or a client to prove you can think, not just execute.

Rumelt's kernel: what a strategy actually is Richard Rumelt's Good Strategy / Bad Strategy defines a strategy as three parts: Diagnosis — what is actually going on. The critical obstacle, named. Not "we need more leads" but "we generate enough leads, and 70% of them are outside our ICP because our only channel rewards volume." Guiding policy — the approach chosen to deal with that obstacle, which necessarily rules out other approaches. "Move spend from broad paid social to intent-based search and partnerships in one vertical." Coherent actions — a small set of steps that support each other rat

A real strategy document is one to three pages. Longer does not get read, and length correlates with vagueness rather than rigour. The annual version takes a week of thinking and an afternoon of writing; the quarterly refresh takes an hour. The time goes into the arithmetic and the arguments about what to drop.

Tactics expire faster than ever; the kernel does not. Channel-specific plans go stale within a year — an argument for a diagnosis-led plan whose actions can be swapped without rewriting the logic. AI removes the excuse for a thin diagnosis. Synthesising reviews, transcripts and competitor messaging is cheap now, so a plan opening with generic market claims looks lazier than it did three years ago. Attribution weakness changes planning. With channel-level measurement degraded (M13, M15), good plans commit to a budget split and a holdout test rather than promising per-channel ROI.

A tactics list with a budget and no diagnosis. Goals presented as strategy. "Grow 40%" tells nobody what to do on Monday. Too many objectives. Three or more priorities means none. Eight channels, no depth. All activation, no brand — profitable for two quarters, then acquisition costs climb and nobody knows why. No kill criteria , so failing initiatives run until someone loses patience.

Write the one-page strategy for your chosen business using templates/marketing-plan-1pager.md , pulling from M02–M05. Diagnosis (10 min). One paragraph naming the single critical obstacle, with evidence. Ban "increase," "improve" and "grow" here — they describe outcomes, not problems. Guiding policy (5 min). One or two sentences, stated so that it excludes something. Coherent actions (10 min). Three to five that support each other. Owner and date on each. Objectives, goals, KPIs (5 min). One objective, two goals with numbers and dates, three KPIs including one leading and one lagging. Budget (

From memory: Rumelt's three parts of a strategy Three symptoms of bad strategy Objective vs goal vs KPI Why channel focus beats channel spread on a small budget 70/20/10 and 60/40, and one caveat on each Two questions that let you say no well
A strategy is a diagnosis, a guiding policy, and coherent actions — and it must say what you will not do. A list of tactics with a budget is not a strategy, however confident the deck looks.

Every channel in Part 2 ends at a page. If that page converts at 1% instead of 3%, you pay triple for every customer, and no amount of ad optimization recovers it. Conversion work is also the cheapest lever you own — no budget approval, no algorithm's cooperation required — which makes it the highest-leverage skill in this course relative to the time it takes to learn.

Owned, earned, paid — and why the distinction is strategic Owned — website, email list, product, customer database. You control it, it survives platform policy changes, and it appreciates. Earned — press, reviews, word of mouth, Reddit mentions, being cited by an AI answer engine. Credible, free, not directly controllable. Paid — ads. Instant, scalable, and it stops the moment you stop paying. You are renting attention. The rule: paid and earned should feed owned. A campaign that generates sales but no email addresses, no reviews, and no returning-visitor cohort bought revenue without building

A CRO cycle on a small site: Pick the page with the most traffic × the worst conversion rate. You cannot learn from a page with 40 visits a month. Watch replays and read the heatmap. Write down three specific observations. Write hypotheses as: Because [evidence], I believe [change] will [effect] measured by [metric]. Rank by impact × confidence ÷ effort. Ship the top one. If traffic is too low for a valid A/B test (M14 — usually true under a few hundred conversions a month), make the change and compare periods, accepting weaker evidence. Do not run a test you cannot power; you will read noise

Your analytics undercount, permanently. Google did not remove third-party cookies from Chrome — it confirmed in April 2025 they stay, then in October 2025 announced it was retiring most Privacy Sandbox technologies (Topics, Protected Audience, Attribution Reporting), deprecated in Chrome 144 (January 2026) and targeted for removal in Chrome 150 (July 2026). Ignore the 2023-era "cookieless future" advice. The real constraints are unchanged: consent (GDPR/ePrivacy) means a share of EU visitors is never measured, Safari's ITP truncates cookie lifetimes, and ad blockers remove more. Server-side ta

Redesigning instead of diagnosing. A redesign changes 50 variables at once, so you learn nothing and often lose conversions you had. Testing button colors. Micro-tests on low-traffic sites waste months. Test offers, headlines, page structure, form length — things big enough to detect. Homepage as landing page for cold paid traffic. Stacking a chat widget, popup, cookie banner, and review carousel , then wondering why mobile LCP is 6 seconds. Optimizing the page when the offer is wrong. If nobody wants it at that price, no layout fixes it (M01, M04). Trusting a "winning" test that ran four days

Pick a real landing page for your chosen business — yours, or a direct competitor's if you have none. Open it on a phone as well as a desktop. Part A — audit (25 min). Score each item Pass / Weak / Fail, with one sentence of evidence: Can you tell what it is, who it is for, and what to do in five seconds? Is there exactly one primary action? Does the headline match the promise of the ad or link that would send traffic here? Is there proof, and is it placed next to the relevant doubt? Are the top three buyer objections answered on the page? How many form fields, and is each one used immediately

Close everything. Diagnose before you change, and change the biggest thing you can measure. Watch ten session replays before you touch a pixel — the problem is almost never the one you assumed, and it is usually the offer, the message match, or the form, not the design.

SEO has the best long-run economics and the worst patience requirements: no cost per click, compounding results, and six to twelve months before you know if it worked. It is also being restructured underneath you. Roughly 60% of Google searches now end without a click to any external site, and when an AI Overview appears the click-through rate of the top organic result drops sharply — roughly halved, per SISTRIX data reported in 2026. Ranking first is no longer the same as getting the visit. That does not make search less valuable. It moves the prize from ranking to being the brand the answer

How search engines work Three stages, each a separate failure point. Crawl — a bot fetches pages, following links and your sitemap. If it cannot reach a page, nothing else matters. Index — the page is parsed, rendered, and stored. Google may crawl and decline to index ("Crawled – currently not indexed" in Search Console), usually judging the page low-value or duplicative. Rank — indexed pages are ordered by hundreds of signals, dominated by relevance to intent, content quality, and off-site authority. How answer engines differ ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot, and Google's AI Overviews wor

A realistic first 90 days on a small site: Week 1 — Set up and verify Google Search Console (free, non-negotiable). Crawl with Screaming Frog. Fix indexation blockers, broken links, missing titles. Weeks 2-3 — Build a keyword map: 20-40 terms grouped into topics, each with an intent, a target URL, and a page type taken from the SERP. Weeks 4-10 — Publish against commercial-intent terms first. Improve existing pages before writing new ones; moving a page from position 8 is faster than starting at zero. Ongoing — Internal links from every new page to your money pages. Pursue mentions: directorie

Publishing volume is not a strategy. AI made competent content free, so the supply of adequate articles is effectively infinite and worth near zero. Only content containing something unavailable elsewhere — proprietary data, real testing, named expertise, an actual opinion — earns links, citations, or trust. Informational traffic is structurally declining. If your model depended on ad revenue from "what is X" articles, it is in trouble. If it depended on reaching buyers, shift to commercial-intent and product-adjacent content. SEO and PR merged. The work that gets you cited by an LLM is the wo

Chasing volume over intent. Ranking for terms whose searchers will never buy. Ignoring the SERP. Writing a product page for a query where Google only shows listicles. Publishing new pages while existing ones rot. Refreshing usually beats creating. Treating technical SEO as the whole job. A perfectly crawlable site with nothing worth reading ranks for nothing. Expecting results in six weeks , then quitting at week ten, right before compounding starts. Stuffing FAQ schema everywhere to "optimize for AI Overviews." Citation follows genuine authority and clear answers, not markup tricks. Reporting

For your chosen business , build a table with these columns: Keyword | Intent (I/C/T/N) | Est. volume | Difficulty (from the actual SERP) | Business value 1-5 | SERP page type | AI Overview present? Who is cited? | Target URL | Have/Need Rules: at least 8 commercial-investigation terms, at least 8 long-tail terms, no navigational terms for other brands. Ranking was the goal; being the cited answer is the goal now. Write clear, extractable answers on commercial-intent topics, make your entity consistent and visible across the third-party sources machines read, and measure share of answer — not sessions.

Content is the cheapest way to create demand and the easiest place to waste a year. Most content programs fail in a specific, predictable way: they produce traffic from people who will never buy, report that traffic as success, and get cut in the first budget review. Knowing the difference between traffic and demand is the whole skill.

Content that captures demand vs. content that creates it Two different jobs, two different formats, two different metrics (M01). Capture content meets people already looking: comparison pages, "alternatives to X", pricing, use-case and integration pages, documentation. Low volume, high intent, converts now. Overlaps heavily with SEO (M08). Creation content reaches people not looking: opinion, original research, teardowns, video, newsletters. High volume, no immediate conversion, and the only way to expand beyond existing search demand. Most teams do neither and produce middle content — generic

A one-person program that works: Keep a running idea list sourced from real customer language — support tickets, sales objections, review sites, community threads. Never brainstorm from scratch. One pillar per week, on a fixed day, at a quality you can repeat. Cut it into five derivatives across your two chosen platforms. Spend Friday distributing and replying. Monthly, check which pieces produced replies, signups, or inbound — not views — and write more of those. Quarterly, kill the platform that produced nothing.

Commodity content is worthless. Anyone can generate a competent 1,500-word explainer in a minute, so competent explainers have no scarcity value and earn no links, citations, or memory. Answer engines strip traffic from informational content. With roughly 60% of Google searches ending without a click, and top-position CTR dropping sharply when an AI Overview appears, "write helpful articles and collect the traffic" is structurally broken for generic topics. So make what only you can make: proprietary data from your own operations, customer stories with real numbers, first-hand testing, genuine

Measuring content by traffic. The metric that most reliably hides failure. Publishing without distributing. Half your hours belong after the publish button. Starting on five platforms. You will sustain none. A blog full of category explainers no buyer ever needed. Posting only from the company LinkedIn page while no named human posts. Entering Reddit to promote. You get banned, and the thread outlives you. Hiring a creator for one post and calling the channel tested. Quitting at month three — content and SEO both pay just past the point most people quit, which is exactly why the returns still

Build a 90-day content plan of 12 pieces for your chosen business (one per week, allowing for slippage). Part A — the plan (35 min). A table with one row per piece: # | Title/angle | Format | Job (capture / create / convert / prove) | Audience & their trigger | Why only we can make this | Primary distribution | 3 derivatives | Success signal Constraints, to force real choices: At least 3 capture pieces tied to keywords from your M08 map At least 2 pieces built on something proprietary — your data, your customers, your testing At least 2 case studies or proof pieces At least 1 opinion piece

Close everything. Write from memory: Capture vs. creation content, with two formats of each, and what "middle content" is The test that tells you whether a planned piece is worth writing What content-market fit looks like and how you would recognize it The pillar-plus-repurposing system and a weekly cadence one person can hold Why publishing is not distributing, and four distribution actions One sentence on the job of each: LinkedIn, short video, YouTube, Reddit Four criteria for evaluating a creator collaboration Why organic reach declines on every platform, and what that implies about email
Produce only what nobody else could produce, then spend half your time distributing it. Traffic is not demand — if you cannot name the reader and the next action, the piece is not worth writing.

Paid search is the purest demand capture (M01). Someone types what they want; you pay to be the answer. That makes it the fastest channel to revenue and the easiest to measure — which is why it is where the most money is quietly wasted. It looks like it works because the conversions land in the report. Whether they would have happened anyway is a different question, and it is the one that gets people promoted or fired.

The auction: you don't pay your bid Ad Rank ≈ bid × ad quality (expected CTR, ad relevance, landing page experience) + expected impact of assets, filtered by context and rank thresholds. You then pay roughly the minimum needed to beat the advertiser below you. Practically: a competitor with better ads and a better landing page outranks you while paying less. Quality is a discount, not a vanity score. Quality Score (1–10, keyword level) reports the same three components — treat it as a diagnostic. Low expected CTR means weak copy for that query; low ad relevance means query and ad don't match;

Computing max CPC. Work backwards from the money. Target CPA €50, landing page converts clicks to leads at 4%: Max CPC = target CPA × conversion rate = €50 × 0.04 = €2.00 If the auction demands €4, you have exactly three options: raise conversion rate (page, offer, form), raise what a conversion is worth (price, LTV, close rate), or don't run in this auction. There is no fourth, and "improve the ad copy" is a rounding error against a 2× gap. For ecommerce, extend one step: €2.00 CPC at 4% CVR means €50 cost per order, so contribution margin must exceed €50 before you even discuss ROAS targets.

Manual targeting is over; input quality is the job. Your leverage is the conversion action you choose, the first-party data you feed, asset quality, and your negatives. The SERP is more answer-shaped. With ~60% of Google searches ending without a click and AI Overviews sharply cutting top-position organic CTR, paid results carry more of the click load — which argues for higher CPCs, not lower. Chrome did not remove third-party cookies. Sending all traffic to the homepage. Kills message match and Quality Score at once. Tracking the wrong event. Optimising to "all form submits" when half are spam teaches the algorithm to find more spam. Over-segmenting into SKAGs. Starves smart bidding. Ignoring the search terms report, then discovering 30% of spend went somewhere irrelevant. Judging PMax by its own report. It grades its own homework. Calling cheap branded CPA "performance." Changing bids and budgets daily. Change one thing, then wait 1–2 weeks or ~30 conversions.

Build a full campaign plan for your chosen business . Spend nothing. Structure. Name campaigns and ad groups. Justify each split by budget or target, not tidiness. Include a brand campaign and state whether you would actually run it. 20 keywords by intent. Label each transactional ("buy", "near me", "pricing"), commercial investigation ("best", "vs", "alternatives"), or informational. Assign a match type and say why. Use Keyword Planner for volume and bid estimates. Negatives. At least 15 terms across account and campaign level, including three you'd only find by imagining how broad match misf

Close everything. Write from memory: Ad Rank in words, and why a competitor can rank above you while paying less. What "exact match" matches in 2026, and your main lever of control. Why granular SKAG structures now hurt performance. The max CPC formula, and your three options when market price exceeds it. The five rungs of the diagnostic ladder, in order. Two ways to control Performance Max.

Paid search rewards arithmetic before cleverness. Compute the max CPC you can afford, decide whether the auction is winnable — and never let a channel's own report be your only evidence that it worked.

Search waits for intent. Paid social interrupts people who weren't looking for you, which makes it the main scalable way to create demand (M01) rather than harvest it. It is also the channel where the platform has taken almost every decision away from you except one: what the ad says and shows. If you learn only one skill here, learn to brief and judge creative — that is now the actual targeting mechanism.

Interruption vs. intent On Google you buy a query. On Meta, TikTok, or YouTube you buy attention from someone mid-scroll. Consequences: conversion rates are lower, CPMs are cheaper, and the ad has to do the work that the search query did for free — establish that a problem exists, that it's theirs, and that you solve it. This is why paid social copy is longer and more emotional than search copy, and why "we ran ads and nobody converted" is usually a creative failure, not a targeting failure. Creative is the targeting Meta's Advantage+ Audience and broad targeting mean the delivery system decid

How CPM × CTR × CVR determines CPA. Only three numbers matter, and every optimisation is one of them. CPM €10 → 1,000 impressions cost €10. CTR 1% → 10 clicks, so CPC = €1.00. Landing page CVR 3% → 0.3 conversions from those 10 clicks. CPA = €10 / 0.3 = €33 . Now double CTR to 2% — better creative, nothing else changes: 20 clicks, 0.6 conversions, CPA = €17 . Creative quality halved your customer acquisition cost without touching targeting or bids. Alternatively hold CTR and lift landing page CVR from 3% to 5%: 0.5 conversions, CPA = €20 . This is why M07 (CRO) and M11 are the same problem vie

Advantage+ made manual detailed targeting largely obsolete in many verticals. Your job moved upstream: creative, offer, first-party data signals, and the optimisation goal you choose. Chrome kept third-party cookies (confirmed April 2025), and Google retired most Privacy Sandbox technologies in October 2025. The constraints that actually degrade your social tracking are consent requirements, Safari ITP, ad blockers, and iOS ATT — which is exactly why server-side CAPI matters and why it isn't going away. AI generation collapsed production cost, not judgment cost. You can produce fifty variation

Choosing the wrong objective and then blaming the creative. Splitting budget across many small ad sets, guaranteeing permanent learning limited status. Testing colours and button text while never testing a genuinely different idea. Killing ads after one day. You need enough conversions to distinguish signal from noise (M14). Judging creative by internal taste. The team hates the ad that works. This happens constantly. Running pixel only, no CAPI. You are optimising on partial data and blaming the algorithm. Uncapped retargeting — high reported ROAS, low real incrementality, annoyed audience. R

For your chosen business : Five creative concepts, genuinely distinct angles. For each, write: the audience, the belief before, the belief after, the hook line (the literal first sentence or first visual), the format, the proof element, and the CTA. Concepts must differ at the idea level — five UGC videos with different scripts is one concept, not five. The test plan. Which concept is the control, what budget and duration, what optimisation event, and what minimum number of conversions you need before you'll judge anything. State in advance the metric that decides the winner, and the kill crit

Close everything. Write from memory: Why creative is now the targeting mechanism. The learning phase threshold and why over-segmenting budget breaks it. The concept/angle/format/variation hierarchy, and where testing budget belongs. The CPM × CTR × CVR chain, and what doubling CTR does to CPA. Hook rate vs. hold rate, and what a high hook / low hold pattern tells you. Why retargeting ROAS overstates its value.
On paid social you are not buying an audience, you are buying attention with an idea — and the idea decides who shows up. Fix the hook before you touch the targeting.

Every other channel is rented. Google changes the SERP, Meta changes the algorithm, TikTok changes what it promotes, and your traffic halves through no decision of yours. An email list is the only audience you own outright — a set of addresses you can reach without paying an intermediary for permission. For most ecommerce and subscription businesses, automated email flows produce a disproportionate share of channel revenue from a small fraction of sends. It is the highest-margin work in marketing and the least glamorous, which is why it is so often neglected.

Building the list without poisoning it A list is only an asset if the people on it want to hear from you. Buying lists, pre-ticked consent boxes, and scraped addresses destroy deliverability for everyone on your domain, permanently. The lead magnet rule that matters: the magnet must be adjacent to the purchase, not merely popular. A €50 Amazon voucher builds a list of people who want vouchers. A "20-point roof inspection checklist" builds a list of people who own roofs and are worried about them. Generic magnets produce big lists with near-zero revenue per recipient, and then the unengaged maj

A weekly rhythm for a small business, roughly 2 hours: Monday — check the previous week's flows: revenue per recipient by flow, unsubscribes, complaint rate, bounce rate. Fix anything trending wrong before you write anything new. Midweek — build one campaign to a segment , not the whole list. Segment first, then write to that segment as if you were writing to one person in it. Monthly — one flow improvement. Add an email, rewrite the weakest one, change a delay, or fix a suppression rule. Flows compound; campaigns don't. Quarterly — list hygiene and a sunset sequence for the unengaged. Tooling

Open rates are decoration. Apple Mail Privacy Protection broke them years ago and they have not recovered. Any advice, agency report, or tool that leads with open rate is out of date — judge on clicks, conversions and revenue per recipient. Authentication is enforced, not advised. Without SPF, DKIM and DMARC aligned, bulk mail to Gmail and Yahoo simply doesn't arrive reliably. First-party email data got more valuable, not less. As ad platforms lose browser signal to consent rules, Safari ITP, ad blockers and iOS ATT, hashed email is the identifier that still works — for customer match audience

A generic lead magnet. Big list, no buyers, degraded reputation. Campaigns but no flows. The flows are where the money is. Blasting the whole list every time because segmenting shrinks the send count. Never removing anyone. Unengaged subscribers actively suppress delivery to engaged ones. Optimising subject lines for opens. You are optimising a broken metric, and clickbait subject lines raise complaints. No plain-text alternative, image-only emails. They break, they look like spam, and they fail accessibility. Treating unsubscribes as failure. An unsubscribe is far better than a spam complaint

For your chosen business : Lead magnet. Write the magnet and one sentence explaining why it is adjacent to the purchase. Then write the alternative generic version, and state exactly what the difference would do to revenue per recipient. The welcome flow — 3 emails, written in full. For each: trigger, delay, subject line, preview text, body, one call to action. Email 1 delivers the promise. Email 2 carries the strongest proof you actually have. Email 3 handles the biggest objection and makes the offer. Keep them shorter than feels comfortable. Lifecycle map. Table it: stage, desired next actio

Close everything. Write from memory: Why a lead magnet must be adjacent to the purchase. The five flows and what each contains. Why open rate is unreliable and what you use instead. SPF, DKIM, DMARC — what each does, and the spam complaint threshold. RFM, and one action for each of two RFM segments. Why an unsubscribe is better than a spam complaint.

The list is the only audience you own — and you keep it by sending less to fewer people, more relevantly. Flows beat campaigns; revenue per recipient beats open rate; complaint rate beats both as a warning.

This is the module that separates people who keep their jobs from people who don't. Anyone can run a campaign. The person who survives the budget review is the one who can say what happened, what it cost, what it produced, and how confident they are — in language a CFO accepts. Marketers get fired for two things: not being able to explain their numbers, and confidently explaining numbers that turn out to be wrong. Both are measurement failures, not campaign failures.

One metric that matters, and the tree beneath it Pick a single number that, if it moves, means the business is working. Then decompose it into the inputs you actually control. That decomposition is the metric tree , and it is the whole job. Ecommerce: Revenue = Sessions × Conversion rate × Average order value. Each branch splits again — sessions by channel, conversion rate by device and landing page. B2B: Pipeline = Leads × Qualification rate × Average deal size, with Leads = Traffic × Form conversion rate. The tree tells you where a change came from. Revenue down 20% is not actionable. Revenu

Reporting cadence. Daily — only anomaly checks. Did tracking break? Is spend pacing? Weekly — channel-level spend, leads or orders, cost per outcome. Look for breakage and trends, not verdicts. Monthly — the decision meeting. What we spent, what it produced, what we learned, what changes. Quarterly — allocation and incrementality (M15). Writing a monthly report a non-marketer can act on. One page, in this order: The headline number vs. target and vs. last month, in currency. Three bullets: what happened and why. Written in cause-and-effect sentences, not metric dumps. A channel table: spend, o

Triangulation is the standard. Three independent lenses: MMM for the portfolio view across all spend including offline, incrementality testing for causal ground truth, and platform attribution for tactical, in-flight signal. Senior decision-makers trust independent incrementality testing more than MMM or in-platform reporting — so the marketer who can run a clean holdout has more credibility than the one with the prettiest dashboard. Branded search and retargeting are where non-incremental spend hides. If you only ever check one thing for incrementality, check those two. Attribution got simple

Reporting metrics instead of decisions. Nobody wants your dashboard; they want to know what to do. Summing platform-reported conversions. You will report more sales than the company made. Reacting to weekly noise and restarting learning phases every Monday. No UTM convention, so half your traffic sits in (other) and nothing can be reconstructed later. Tracking everything and defining nothing. Two hundred events, no agreed key event. Confusing correlation with cause. Spend went up, revenue went up — in Q4, when revenue always goes up. Trusting last-click and defunding the demand-creation channe

For your chosen business : Metric tree. Define the one metric that matters, then decompose it two levels down. Mark each node leading or lagging, and circle the two nodes you can actually influence next month. Key events. List the 3–6 events you would track in GA4, with parameters and assigned values. State which single one is the primary key event for optimisation, and why the others are not. UTM convention. Write it as a one-page standard: allowed medium values (a closed list), the campaign naming pattern with a date convention, casing rules, and who owns the spreadsheet. Then write three co

Close everything. Write from memory: The metric tree for your business, two levels deep. Three ways GA4's model differs from Universal Analytics. The five UTM parameters and two rules that prevent broken data. What last-click over-credits, what view-through over-credits, and how many attribution models GA4 retains. Why platform conversions never sum to actual revenue. The three legs of measurement triangulation, and which one senior decision-makers trust most.

No single measurement method is true; the skill is knowing the direction each one lies in. Report decisions rather than metrics, state your confidence out loud, and treat platform numbers as signal rather than truth. Part 2 gave you the channels. Part 3 gives you the judgment to allocate across them — starting with how to run a test that will not lie to you, then M15, where incrementality testing and media mix modelling turn the honest uncertainty above into a defensible budget.

M13 ended on an uncomfortable note: no measurement method is true. Experimentation is the exception. A properly randomised test is the only tool in marketing that produces a causal answer rather than a correlational story. It is also the tool most often used badly. Most "A/B tests" in industry are underpowered, stopped early, judged on the wrong metric, or not randomised at all — producing confident conclusions that are noise. Knowing when a test can answer your question, and when you do not have the traffic to run one at all, is a senior skill few people acquire.

A hypothesis is a sentence with four parts Not "let's try a green button." A usable hypothesis reads: Because [evidence], we expect [specific change] to cause [effect on one metric], measured by [metric, over what period]. Worked: Because 61% of session recordings show users scrolling past the pricing table without stopping, we expect a three-tier comparison with a recommended plan to increase trial starts, measured by trial-start rate per session over four weeks. The "because" is the part that matters. Tests grounded in evidence — recordings, interviews, support tickets, funnel drop-off — win

The test log. Organisations fail to learn from testing because results live in a screenshot in someone's Slack. Keep one shared table, one row per test, permanently: ID Date Area Hypothesis Primary metric MDE Sample Result & CI Decision What we now believe The last column makes it an asset. Not "variant B won," but "customers respond to risk-reversal more than to discounting — third time we've seen it." Losses are entries too; a documented loss stops the same idea being re-proposed every year. Velocity vs quality. Both fail alone. High velocity with sloppy method produces a fast stream of

Platform-side testing is the norm for ads. Meta's A/B tool and Google's experiments handle randomisation, but inherit black-box optimisation: Advantage+ and Performance Max reallocate delivery mid-test, and the platform judges on its own attributed conversions. Treat platform experiments as directional; treat geo holdouts and conversion lift studies as evidence (M15). AI made variant production nearly free and hypothesis quality the bottleneck. You can generate fifty ad variations in a morning; your traffic did not multiply by fifty. Testing capacity is unchanged — but there is no longer any e

No pre-registered primary metric, so the winner is chosen after the fact from whichever number looks best. Stopping the moment it hits 95%. Manufactured wins. Testing trivia. Button colours on 400 sessions a week. Ignoring MDE , running a test that could never have detected the effect, and concluding "no difference." Running partial weeks, so Tuesday-heavy traffic decides the outcome. Not checking the guardrails — lifting leads while destroying lead quality. Never re-testing a big winner and building strategy on a fluke. No test log, so the same idea is retested every eighteen months as staff

For your chosen business : Three hypotheses in the because/we-expect/measured-by format, each grounded in a specific piece of evidence you can name. If you have no evidence, your first task is not a test — write down how you would get it. Sample size reality check. Take your top hypothesis. Write down your real baseline conversion rate and weekly traffic. Compute the sample needed for a 10% relative lift, then for a 25% lift. State how many weeks each would take, and conclude honestly whether you can test at all. If you cannot test , write the alternative plan: which two of bigger swings / pai

Close everything. Write from memory: The four parts of a hypothesis. Why before-after comparisons are usually invalid, and the two cases where they are acceptable. What happens to required sample size when you halve the effect you want to detect. What a p-value of 0.04 does and does not mean. What peeking does to a test, and what a stopping rule contains. Four things to do when you lack the traffic to test.

Run the sample size calculation before you design the test, not after. It tells you whether the question can be answered at all — and if it cannot, the honest move is a bigger change, a qualitative method, or a decision made on judgment with the reasoning written down.

This is the module that changes what you are worth. Anyone can run a campaign; the person who decides where the money goes, and defends it to a CFO, is doing the senior job. The central idea is one sentence: attribution tells you what happened after a click; it cannot tell you what would have happened without the ad. That gap is where most marketing budgets quietly leak.

How budgets actually get set Percent of revenue. A fixed share of last year's or forecast revenue — commonly 5–12% depending on category and margin. Easy, stable, and backwards: it cuts spend exactly when sales fall and you most need demand. A sanity constraint, never a rationale. Competitive parity. Match a competitor's share of voice. Its merit is that share of voice and share of market track each other over time, so sustained under-investment tends to cost share. Its flaw is assuming your competitor knows what they are doing and shares your objectives, margins and awareness. Objective-and-t

A worked reallocation Ecommerce, £40,000/month, 60% gross margin, break-even ROAS 1.67×. Channel Spend Reported ROAS Evidence Branded search £4,000 9.0× No holdout ever run Non-brand search £12,000 3.1× Marginal ROAS on last £3k: 1.9× Meta prospecting £14,000 1.8× Geo holdout showed real lift Retargeting £6,000 6.5× No holdout ever run Creative production £2,000 — Two new concepts/month Brand video £2,000 — Cut last quarter, being restored Run the cheap holdouts first. Four weeks: retargeting off in one matched region, branded search off in another. Suppose retargeting comes back 30% increment

Cookies did not die. Chrome kept third-party cookies (confirmed April 2025), and most Privacy Sandbox technologies were retired in October 2025 — deprecated in Chrome 144 (January 2026), removal targeted for Chrome 150 (July 2026). GDPR and ePrivacy obligations are unchanged. The measurement gap comes from consent rejection, ITP, ad blockers and ATT — strengthening the case for geo tests and MMM, neither of which needs user-level data. Black-box buying moved the budget question up a level. With Performance Max and Advantage+ the algorithm allocates to keywords and placements, not you. You stil

Allocating on average ROAS instead of marginal return. Scaling the channel with the best reported number, usually the least incremental one. Never running a single holdout, then arguing about attribution models for years. Cutting brand spend in a downturn and mistaking the following two quarters' decline for a market problem. Setting the budget as a percentage and having no argument when asked why. Judging an MMM by how good the numbers look rather than whether spend varied enough for it to learn. Reallocating and then judging it on channel ROAS, which will get worse by construction.

For your chosen business : Build the budget objective-and-task style. From a customer or revenue target, back through your M05 funnel rates, costing each line. Compare the total to a percent-of-revenue sanity check. Split creation vs capture and justify the ratio in two sentences, given your awareness level, category and cash position. Sketch the saturation curve for your largest channel and mark where marginal return crosses break-even ROAS or max CPA. Design one cheap holdout: which slice, how long, what you measure from your own data, what result would change your allocation, and what it co

Close everything. Write from memory: Three ways budgets get set, and which is defensible. Why "scale what works" fails, in terms of average vs marginal return. What an incremental conversion is, and three ways to measure it. The two places non-incremental spend hides, and why. What MMM needs, one thing it is good at, one it is bad at. The three legs of triangulation, ranked by trust. The 60/40 heuristic and two conditions that shift it.

Attribution tells you what happened after a click; only a holdout tells you what would have happened without the ad. Before you scale the channel with the best reported return, turn it off somewhere and find out what you actually bought.

title: B2B vs B2C and Sales Alignment

sections.excerpt: Everything in Parts 1 and 2 applies to both, but the shape of the problem differs enough that applying B2C instincts to a B2B business — or the reverse — reliably wastes a year. There is also a practical reason. Most well-paid marketing jobs are in B2B, and most beginners arrive with only the consumer intuitions they have from being consumers. Talking fluently about buying committees, pipeline math and an MQL SLA is a large share of what makes a junior candidate sound credible.

Buying committees: nobody buys alone In consumer marketing you persuade one person. In B2B, any purchase of size involves a group — commonly cited research on complex B2B buying puts typical committees in the range of six to eleven people, more for enterprise. Each has a different question: Economic buyer: what is the return, and what is the risk to me? User / champion: does this improve my daily work, and can I sell it internally? Technical evaluator: does it integrate, and is it secure? Procurement: price, terms, contract risk. Security / legal: what could go wrong? The blocker: often whoeve

A functioning B2B marketing–sales relationship has five artefacts, and you can audit any company by asking for them: A written ICP and a target account list derived from it (M02). Agreed stage definitions and an SLA with commitments both ways. A pipeline model shared with sales and finance, updated with real rates each quarter. A closed-loop report : which sources produced opportunities and revenue, not leads. A recurring joint meeting reviewing rejected leads, lost-deal reasons, and what buyers actually said. The fifth is where the compounding happens. Marketers who sit in on sales calls writ

Black-box ad platforms punish bad lead definitions. Performance Max and Advantage+ optimise toward whatever conversion you feed them: feed "form fill" and they find the cheapest form-fillers alive. Feed offline conversion imports back from the CRM — SQLs and closed-won, with values — and the same algorithms work in your favour. In B2B, the offline conversion feed is the highest-leverage technical task in paid media. AI search changed how committees research. With ~60% of Google searches ending click-free and AI Overviews cutting top-result CTR sharply, buyers arrive later and better informed,

Optimising for MQL volume with no visibility into what happens after the handoff. One message for the whole committee, usually written for the user and useless to the CFO. Ignoring "do nothing" as the main competitor. Gating everything, suppressing reach and filling the CRM with curiosity. No SLA, so lead quality is an argument rather than a measurable. A pipeline model with no sales capacity check, then surprise that leads sat untouched. Cutting brand spend in B2B because it does not produce this quarter's MQLs, then wondering why win rates fall. Never listening to a sales call.

For your chosen business (if it is B2C, do questions 1 and 6 for a plausible B2B version — this is a transferable-skill exercise): Map the buying committee. Every role, the one question each asks, and the single asset that answers it. Mark the likeliest blocker. Write your stage definitions : MQL, SAL, SQL, Opportunity — one sentence each, with the specific behaviour or firmographic that qualifies. Draft the SLA in five lines: marketing's volume and quality commitment, sales' response time, attempts, disposition requirement, joint review cadence. Do the pipeline math. From a revenue target, us

Close everything. Write from memory: Four roles on a buying committee and what each cares about. The 95-5 rule and its two implications for how you spend and how you measure. Lead gen vs demand gen, and why gated lead gen degrades. MQL, SAL, SQL — and what the SAL stage exists for. The pipeline math backwards from a revenue target, and the two constraints people forget. When ABM is worth it and when it is not. Three things that differ between B2B and B2C, and two that transfer.

In B2B you are selling to a committee that is mostly not in the market, whose default is to do nothing. So the work is being remembered until the trigger fires, and giving your champion the material to win an internal argument you will never attend.

Acquisition is rented. Every customer you buy, you buy again next month at a slightly higher price, because auctions get more competitive and the easy audience is exhausted first. Retention is owned. A customer who stays gives you revenue with no acquisition cost, which raises LTV, which raises the CAC you can afford, which lets you outbid competitors for the same click. That is the whole strategic argument, and it is why the highest-leverage marketing work in most companies is not in the ad account. It is also the argument nobody makes in the budget meeting, because retention improvements are

Retention multiplies everything Take a subscription at £50/month with 60% gross margin. 8% monthly churn → lifetime 1 / 0.08 = 12.5 months → LTV (gross profit) = £50 × 0.60 × 12.5 = £375 5% churn → 20 months → £600 3% churn → 33.3 months → £1,000 Cutting churn from 8% to 5% raised LTV by 60%. From 8% to 3% it nearly tripled it. Now convert that into acquisition power. At a 3:1 LTV:CAC target, max CAC goes £125 → £200 → £333. At £375 LTV you cannot profitably buy a customer at £150; at £1,000 you can outbid almost everyone in your category, run channels competitors find unaffordable, and still

Worked example. A £45/month subscription, 65% gross margin, 7% monthly churn, CAC £160. Lifetime 14.3 months. LTV = £45 × 0.65 × 14.3 = £418 . LTV:CAC = 2.6:1. Payback = £160 / £29.25 = 5.5 months . Workable, not comfortable. Diagnosis: cohort analysis shows 41% of churn happens in the first 60 days, and customers who connect their calendar in week one retain at nearly twice the rate. Activation metric: calendar connected within 7 days. Current rate: 38%. Interventions: move the connection into the signup flow, add a one-click integration, send a day-2 nudge with a 90-second video, give human

Rising acquisition costs make retention the arbitrage. With buying automated (Performance Max, Advantage+), most competitors run similar algorithms against similar audiences, so targeting cleverness is largely gone as an edge. Being able to pay more per customer than your competitor is one of the few remaining structural advantages. First-party data is now an input to the ad platforms, not just a mailing list. Customer lists, offline conversion imports and value-based bidding signals are how you steer black boxes, so a well-maintained owned audience improves acquisition performance directly. Z

Reporting an average retention rate instead of cohort curves, hiding every trend that matters. Computing LTV on revenue instead of gross profit, then over-spending on the strength of a number 40% too high. Projecting LTV to infinity on a constant-churn assumption. Confusing logo and revenue churn and misdiagnosing which customers you are losing. Chasing a correlated activation metric and pushing users toward a behaviour that never caused anything. Launching a referral programme to fix bad word of mouth. Calling a referral programme a network effect. Discounting to reduce churn, which retains p

For your chosen business : Build a cohort table. Six monthly cohorts, retention at months 1, 3 and 6 — real numbers if you have them, estimates if not. Answer in one sentence: does the curve flatten, and at what level? Churn to LTV to max CAC. Compute current churn, average lifetime, LTV on gross profit, and max CAC at your chosen ratio. Recompute with a 25% relative churn improvement and state the change in max CAC and payback. Name your activation metric — the specific first-week or first-order behaviour you believe predicts retention — and how you would test whether it is causal rather than

Close everything. Write from memory: Why a churn improvement raises the CAC you can afford, with the arithmetic. Logo churn vs revenue churn, and what NRR above 100% means. What a flattening cohort curve tells you and what a non-flattening one tells you. Time-to-value and activation metric, and the trap in choosing an activation metric. Four growth loops with one concrete example each. A loop vs a network effect. Three features of referral programmes that work.

Retention sets the price you can afford to pay for a customer. Every point of churn you remove raises max CAC, opens channels your competitors cannot afford, and compounds across every future cohort — which no ad optimisation ever does.

Two opposite errors are common in 2026, and both are expensive. The first is treating AI as a novelty and doing by hand work a model does in seconds. That person is several times slower than a competent peer at the same job, and it shows in output volume. The second is treating AI as a strategy: publishing 400 undifferentiated articles, generating ad copy with no positioning behind it, and being confused when nothing works. Production was never the scarce resource; being worth reading was. This module draws the line — where AI creates leverage, where it destroys value, and what a working proce

Where AI genuinely creates leverage Research synthesis. Reading 60 competitor pages, 200 reviews or a market report and returning a structured summary. The bottleneck was reading time, and that is what a model removes. Verify claims that matter. First drafts, never final ones. A draft is faster to fix than a blank page is to fill; the value is in the editing that follows. Creative variant production. Ten headline angles, six hooks, five image concepts for one offer. In an Advantage+ / Performance Max world, creative volume and diversity is the main input you control (M11, M15) — the clearest R

A realistic week: Monday. The agent-assembled weekly report is in your inbox; you spend 20 minutes interpreting it rather than building it. An anomaly flag catches a landing page's conversion tag that stopped firing on Thursday. Tuesday. Two customer interviews, done by you. Afterwards, transcripts clustered against the last twenty with verbatim quotes pulled. Wednesday. Creative sprint. Context file plus three winning ads plus this month's angle → 40 headline variants. You cut to six worth testing, rewriting four yourself. Thursday. Analysis: SQL written with AI help, cohort retention pulled

The ad platforms are already AI, and that is where most of the impact is. Performance Max, AI Max for Search and Advantage+ made buying input-driven. Your leverage is offer, creative, first-party data and the optimisation goal you choose (M15). Getting good at feeding those systems matters more than any content tool. Content abundance made distribution the constraint. Everyone can produce; almost nobody can reach. Owned audiences (M17), partnerships and genuine authority are worth more than before, not less. AEO/GEO is real and immature. Treat vendor claims sceptically — there is little settle

Publishing AI drafts unedited. Detectable, generic, and it teaches your audience to skip you. No context file, so every output is average-of-the-internet. Trusting statistics the model produced. Every number needs a source. Outsourcing the customer contact and losing the texture that makes copy specific. Volume as a strategy. 400 posts nobody needed. Prompting for polish instead of range. Ask for wider options, then choose. Automating reporting interpretation, not just assembly. Fake reviews, testimonials or synthetic customers presented as real. Legally dangerous and brand-fatal. Learning pro

For your chosen business : Build the context file (15 minutes — the bulk of this exercise). One to two pages: company, ICP, positioning, message hierarchy, voice rules with at least three "never say" items, real proof assets, forbidden claims, two on-brand examples. Save it where you will reuse it. Run one real task with it. Generate ten ad headlines or five subject lines using the context file plus the five-component prompt structure. Cut to two and rewrite them in your own words. Note what the model got wrong — that gap is what you know and it does not. Draw your leverage/destruction line. T

Close everything. Write from memory: Four places AI creates genuine leverage, and what they have in common. Four ways AI destroys value, including the subtle one about customer contact. The three-step workflow and what breaks if you skip each human step. The five components of a strong marketing prompt. What goes in a context file. Why answer-engine visibility argues for original content rather than more AI content. Four skills that appreciate as production is commoditised.

AI removed the cost of production, not the cost of being worth attention. Use it for volume, structure and speed; keep strategy, customer contact and the final judgment yourself — because that is the part that is now scarce, and therefore the part that gets paid.

Nobody can see what you know. They can only see what you produce. Eighteen modules of understanding are worth very little in a job interview, a client conversation, or a bank meeting until they are compressed into a document that shows judgment. This module produces that document — a go-to-market plan for one real business, written to the standard a hiring manager, a client, or a co-founder would take seriously. Writing also forces integration. You will discover in the next two hours that your positioning does not survive contact with your channel choice, or that your unit economics rule out t

A 6–10 page go-to-market plan for one business, written for a reader who is smart, busy, and not a marketer — a CEO, an investor, a client, or an interviewer. Standards: Decisions, not options. "We will do X because Y" beats "we could consider X, Y or Z." A plan that refuses to choose is not a plan. Numbers everywhere they belong. Prices, conversion rates, CAC, CPA ceilings, budget lines, targets. Estimates are fine; unlabelled estimates are not. Mark each assumption as measured, benchmarked, or guessed. Explicit exclusions. What you are not doing, and why, is the strongest signal of judgment

1. Situation and diagnosis (~1 page) What the business is, what it sells, to whom, at what price, and how it makes money today. Then the diagnosis: the single most important constraint on growth , stated as a constraint rather than a wish (M01, M06). "We need more sales" is not a diagnosis. "We convert 4% of demo requests to paid, against a 12% category norm, and we have no idea why" is. "Nobody in our category knows we exist and 90% of our leads come from one referral partner" is. Everything downstream should follow from this sentence — if a later section does not address the constraint, ask

As a portfolio piece. Strip anything confidential, put it in a clean PDF, and make it the thing you send when someone asks what you can do. One well-reasoned plan beats a list of courses you have taken. In job interviews. You will be asked "how would you approach marketing for us?" Do not answer generically — answer with your method, demonstrated: "Here is a plan I built end to end; let me walk you through how I diagnosed the constraint and why I excluded three channels." Then be ready for the pressure test — where the numbers came from, what you would do at half the budget, how you would know

You are now, genuinely, more useful than most people who list marketing on their CV — because you can do the arithmetic, you know what attribution cannot tell you, and you know what you do not know. What you do not have is reps. Judgment comes from having been wrong in specific, memorable ways, and thirty hours cannot manufacture that. The next step is one real thing, run for one quarter, measured honestly: a small budget you actually spend, a landing page you actually ship, an email flow that actually sends, a holdout you actually run. Then write down what surprised you. That log is worth mor

Thirty hours gave you literacy and a working set of models: demand creation versus capture, positioning against alternatives including doing nothing, unit economics that constrain what you can spend, the direction each measurement method lies in, and the fact that only a holdout answers the causal question. Those do not expire when the channels change. Thirty hours did not give you craft. You have not written 200 ads and watched most of them fail.
